2:30.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ رَبُّكَ لِلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةِ إِنِّي جَاعِلࣱ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ خَلِيفَةࣰۖ قَالُوٓاْ أَتَجۡعَلُ فِيهَا مَن يُفۡسِدُ فِيهَا وَيَسۡفِكُ ٱلدِّمَآءَ وَنَحۡنُ نُسَبِّحُ بِحَمۡدِكَ وَنُقَدِّسُ لَكَۖ قَالَ إِنِّيٓ أَعۡلَمُ مَا لَا تَعۡلَمُونَ
2:30.en: And when thy Lord said unto the angels: Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth, they said: Wilt thou place therein one who will do harm therein and will shed blood, while we, we hymn Thy praise and sanctify Thee? He said: Surely I know that which ye know not

15:28.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ رَبُّكَ لِلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةِ إِنِّي خَٰلِقُۢ بَشَرࣰ ا مِّن صَلۡصَٰلࣲ مِّنۡ حَمَإࣲ مَّسۡنُونࣲ‏
15:28.en: And (remember) when thy Lord said unto the angels: Lo! I am creating a mortal out of potter's clay of black mud altered

24:12.ar: لَّوۡلَآ إِذۡ سَمِعۡتُمُوهُ ظَنَّ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنُونَ وَٱلۡمُؤۡمِنَٰتُ بِأَنفُسِهِمۡ خَيۡرࣰ ا وَقَالُواْ هَٰذَآ إِفۡكࣱ مُّبِينࣱ‏
24:12.en: Why did not the believers, men and women, when ye heard it, think good of their own own folk, and say: It is a manifest untruth

7:12.ar: قَالَ مَا مَنَعَكَ أَلَّا تَسۡجُدَ إِذۡ أَمَرۡتُكَۖ قَالَ أَنَا۠ خَيۡرࣱ مِّنۡهُ خَلَقۡتَنِي مِن نَّارࣲ وَخَلَقۡتَهُۥ مِن طِينࣲ‏
7:12.en: He said: What hindered thee that thou didst not fall prostrate when I bade thee? (Iblis) said: I am better than him. Thou createdst me of fire while him Thou didst create of mud

38:75.ar: قَالَ يَٰٓإِبۡلِيسُ مَا مَنَعَكَ أَن تَسۡجُدَ لِمَا خَلَقۡتُ بِيَدَيَّۖ أَسۡتَكۡبَرۡتَ أَمۡ كُنتَ مِنَ ٱلۡعَالِينَ
38:75.en: He said: O Iblis! What hindereth thee from falling prostrate before that which I have created with both My hands? Art thou too proud or art thou of the high exalted

17:62.ar: قَالَ أَرَءَيۡتَكَ هَٰذَا ٱلَّذِي كَرَّمۡتَ عَلَيَّ لَئِنۡ أَخَّرۡتَنِ إِلَىٰ يَوۡمِ ٱلۡقِيَٰمَةِ لَأَحۡتَنِكَنَّ ذُرِّيَّتَهُۥٓ إِلَّا قَلِيلࣰ ا
17:62.en: He said: Seest Thou this (creature) whom Thou hast honoured above me, if Thou give me grace until the Day of Resurrection I verily will seize his seed, save but a few

17:64.ar: وَٱسۡتَفۡزِزۡ مَنِ ٱسۡتَطَعۡتَ مِنۡهُم بِصَوۡتِكَ وَأَجۡلِبۡ عَلَيۡهِم بِخَيۡلِكَ وَرَجِلِكَ وَشَارِكۡهُمۡ فِي ٱلۡأَمۡوَٰلِ وَٱلۡأَوۡلَٰدِ وَعِدۡهُمۡۚ وَمَا يَعِدُهُمُ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنُ إِلَّا غُرُورًا
17:64.en: And excite any of them whom thou canst with thy voice, and urge thy horse and foot against them, and be a partner in their wealth and children, and promise them. Satan promiseth them only to deceive

17:65.ar: إِنَّ عِبَادِي لَيۡسَ لَكَ عَلَيۡهِمۡ سُلۡطَٰنࣱۚ وَكَفَىٰ بِرَبِّكَ وَكِيلࣰ ا
17:65.en: Lo! My (faithful) bondmen - over them thou hast no power, and thy Lord sufficeth as (their) guardian

7:16.ar: قَالَ فَبِمَآ أَغۡوَيۡتَنِي لَأَقۡعُدَنَّ لَهُمۡ صِرَٰطَكَ ٱلۡمُسۡتَقِيمَ
7:16.en: He said: Now, because Thou hast sent me astray, verily I shall lurk in ambush for them on Thy Right Path

zoY0gXXhSM8.speaker: adnan
zoY0gXXhSM8.speaker_note: his Tazkiyah self-value series; refers to his own medical oncology work and his teacher in Syria
zoY0gXXhSM8.title: Tazkiyah Halaqah: Self-Value, Episode 43
zoY0gXXhSM8.one_line: Arrogance feeds on bad assumptions about people; understanding others without accepting or agreeing, illustrated by Iblis, Abu Jahl and serving someone you dislike.
zoY0gXXhSM8.summary: Continuing the self-value module, he restates the foundation: Allah created all people equal and every person, at every moment, can rise to the highest ranks or fall to the lowest. Once this is accepted there is nothing left to prove, and motivation must come from Jannah and Allah's pleasure rather than comparison, which feels dull at first, like coming off a drug. Living by the truth beats living a comfortable lie, and honesty about oneself is a condition for connecting with Allah. He then turns to arrogance as a relationship with others: we fill the gaps in other people's stories with assumptions, and the ego fills them with bad ones so it can rank people beneath itself. The rule is no assumptions, and if one must assume, assume good, except where one is a caregiver or protector. Arrogance dehumanizes, and racism is collective arrogance. He distinguishes understanding from accepting and agreeing, and applies it to Iblis, Abu Jahl's tribal pride, non-Muslims and the LGBTQ movement. He closes with Iblis's reply to Allah, his misjudgment of Adam's clay, and his vow to lead humanity astray by the same arrogance. He invites the audience to serve someone they genuinely dislike.

outline.heading: Self-value and the pendulum between arrogance and inferiority
outline.gist: Most diseases of the heart trace back to a confused sense of self-value; people swing between vanity and low self-esteem until late in life.

outline.heading: All created equal, all with constant potential
outline.gist: Allah gave no one an innate advantage, and anyone can head to the highest or lowest ranks at any moment; this simple fact reshapes how we judge ourselves.

outline.heading: Divine value needs no proving; the parenting trap
outline.gist: Your value is granted at birth and untouched by applause or hatred. Pampered children lose motivation, while parents who make children prove themselves can leave a lasting sense of unworthiness.

outline.heading: Motives Allah provides and the dullness of quitting comparison
outline.gist: Jannah, Allah's love and the identities of steward and servant are the real motives. Giving up the high of feeling better than others feels flat at first, like recovering from addiction.

outline.heading: The truth is better than a comfortable lie
outline.gist: Discovering years of a spouse's betrayal and the Eastern practice of hiding a fatal diagnosis show that people would rather know the truth than live a lie.

outline.heading: Honesty about yourself as the door to connecting with Allah
outline.gist: We struggle to feel the Quran because we need a false problem to react to; clarity about who we are is required to speak to al-Haqq, and feeling better when others fail means feeling worse when they succeed.

outline.heading: Arrogance runs on assumptions: filling in the gaps
outline.gist: We never know anyone's full story, so we fill the gaps, and we fill them badly when we feel threatened. Even who we choose to listen to rests on assumptions.

outline.heading: No assumptions, and if you must, good ones
outline.gist: Ideally you are too busy to assume anything about others; having time for it is a time-management problem.

outline.heading: When bad assumptions are obligatory
outline.gist: Caregivers and protectors must assume the worst: a parent about a child, a business owner about a new partner, a father about a suitor.

outline.heading: The ego's ranking system
outline.gist: The nafs compares looks, wealth and education, and if it finds no flaw it digs into character or religiosity, or seizes on one smirk, so it can place the other person beneath it.

outline.heading: Arrogance dehumanizes; racism as collective arrogance
outline.gist: Every person is a full story; refusing to humanize them is arrogance, and racism does the same to whole peoples, which is how mass killing on this land and elsewhere was justified.

outline.heading: Iblis: would you have obeyed in his place?
outline.gist: Iblis knew Allah and had reached the highest piety, yet refused. Saying we would never have failed is the same arrogance; we can only hope and make dua.

outline.heading: Good assumptions in the slander of Aisha
outline.gist: The Quran rebukes those who did not think well of their own; Abu Ayyub and his wife reasoned that since they would not do it, Aisha and Safwan surely did not.

outline.heading: Understanding versus accepting versus agreeing
outline.gist: Understanding how a wrong could happen is not accepting it as right or agreeing it fit the situation; he asks only for understanding, which is not legitimizing.

outline.heading: How Iblis's arrogance built up
outline.gist: He slowly credited himself for his rank, then faced a new creation honoured as steward of the earth and filled the gaps with bad thoughts about Adam until he refused a direct command.

outline.heading: Abu Jahl and the tribal rivalry with Banu Hashim
outline.gist: Raised to compete with Banu Hashim, Abu Jahl admitted the Prophet was truthful but would never follow a man of that clan; we carry the same arrogance and are simply not tested.

outline.heading: The exercise: serve someone you dislike
outline.gist: His teacher made him serve a man who had made his life hard; once he stopped dehumanizing him and imagined his story, the man became a lifelong friend. He invites the audience to try it honestly.

outline.heading: Understanding people of other faiths
outline.gist: We neither agree with nor accept other creeds, but must understand them or we will generalize and dehumanize; all humanity is the Prophet's ummah, some yet to respond.

outline.heading: Understanding the LGBTQ movement to guard against it
outline.gist: Calling it senseless leaves Muslims without tools; understanding where it comes from is how you protect yourself, not a step toward acceptance.

outline.heading: "What prevented you?" and "I am better than him"
outline.gist: Allah's question hints that something grew inside Iblis and stopped him; he answered with superiority of essence, and did not even dare cite his own piety.

outline.heading: Misjudging Adam's clay
outline.gist: What Iblis saw as inferior, rotting mud, was Adam's strength: the mix of earth and spirit that gives humans unique abilities, as life grows from wet, rotting soil.

outline.heading: Arrogant, or truly superior?
outline.gist: Allah asks whether Iblis grew arrogant or is by nature high; no creation is innately superior, so the only answer is arrogance, and Iblis left it unanswered.

outline.heading: Iblis's respite and his vow against humanity
outline.gist: He asks for time to prove humans unworthy and to lead them like donkeys; Allah grants it but says he has no authority over His true servants. His main trick is to make us arrogant as he was.

themes.label: Self-value, self-worth, confidence
themes.note: Equal creation and constant potential mean there is nothing to prove; worth is divine and fixed.

themes.label: Humility vs vanity and arrogance
themes.note: Arrogance toward others rests on bad assumptions and the ego's ranking system, and it dehumanizes.

themes.label: Shaytan: his methods and how to resist him
themes.note: Iblis fell through arrogance despite great knowledge of Allah; assuming we would have done better repeats his error.

themes.label: Shaytan: his methods and how to resist him
themes.note: His answer to Allah, his misjudgment of Adam, and his vow to misguide people through the same arrogance.

themes.label: Human equality and racism
themes.note: Racism is collective arrogance that dehumanizes whole groups to justify killing them.

themes.label: Tolerance, pluralism and dealing with difference
themes.note: Understanding is distinct from accepting and agreeing; applied to Abu Jahl, a disliked person, other faiths and the LGBTQ movement.

themes.label: Truthfulness and honesty
themes.note: People prefer the truth to a lie, and honesty about oneself is needed to connect with Allah.

themes.label: Parenting and raising children
themes.note: Both pampering and making children constantly prove themselves distort their sense of worth.

Adam created from altered, rotting mud, the basis of Iblis's contempt.
Believers should have thought well of their own when they heard the slander.
"What prevented you from prostrating?" and Iblis's reply "I am better than him."
Allah asks whether Iblis became arrogant or is of the exalted.
Iblis asks for respite, vowing to bring Adam's descendants under his control.
Allah lets him rally his forces but he has no authority over Allah's servants.
Iblis vows to sit on the straight path to misguide people.

hadith.gist: The Prophet encouraged beautifying the Quran with one's voice.

maxims: Your value is divine; no one can touch it
No assumptions; if you must, assume good
Racism is collective arrogance
Understanding is not accepting, and not agreeing
Feel better when others fail, feel less when they succeed

stories.who: Iblis and the command to prostrate to Adam
stories.point: Arrogance can grow until it blocks obedience to a direct command from Allah; no one should assume they are immune.

stories.who: Abu Ayyub al-Ansari and his wife during the slander of Aisha
stories.point: They judged others by themselves and kept a good assumption.

stories.who: Abu Jahl's rivalry with Banu Hashim
stories.point: He knew the Prophet was truthful but tribal pride kept him from following him to the grave.

stories.who: The sheikh serving a man he disliked in Syria
stories.point: Humanizing someone you resent dissolves the resentment; the man became a close friend.

contemporary: The killing of Indigenous peoples on this land as an example of dehumanization
Withholding fatal cancer diagnoses from patients in the Middle East
Muslims as a minority among many faiths in Canada
takeaways: Stop trying to prove your worth; draw motivation from Allah's pleasure and Jannah instead.
Avoid assumptions about people, and assume good unless you are responsible for protecting someone.
Never assume you would have done better than Iblis or other people who fell; hope and make dua.
Learn to understand people without accepting or agreeing with their choices.
Choose someone you truly dislike and serve them for a period.

__9DNgEJVqE.title: Moderation #3: Salman and Abu al-Darda
__9DNgEJVqE.one_line: Salman's visit to Abu al-Darda: your Lord, your family and your body each have a right, so give each its due.
__9DNgEJVqE.summary: The sheikh calls the story of Salman al-Farisi and Abu al-Darda one of the most powerful on moderation. The Prophet had paired them as brothers, Salman from the emigrants and Abu al-Darda from the Ansar. Visiting, Salman found Umm al-Darda neglected and was told her husband had no interest in worldly life. Abu al-Darda offered food but said he was fasting; Salman refused to eat until he ate. At night Salman twice told him to sleep, then woke him near dawn to pray together, and told him that his Lord, his family and his own self each have a right over him, so he must give each its due. When they went to the Prophet, he confirmed that Salman was right. The sheikh explains that Abu al-Darda had begun living without relations with his wife, fasting daily and praying all night to draw closer to Allah. Salman, a seasoned seeker who had travelled the earth in search of truth before Islam, recognised that this was not balanced. Being truly religious, the sheikh says, means honouring the rights of Allah, spouse, children, relatives and body together. He closes by reading the full narration from Bukhari.

outline.heading: A story that summarises moderation
outline.gist: Introduces the narration of Abu Juhayfah about the brotherhood the Prophet formed between Salman and Abu al-Darda.

outline.heading: Salman's visit: the neglected wife, the meal and the night
outline.gist: Salman finds Umm al-Darda neglected, makes Abu al-Darda break his voluntary fast, and makes him sleep before praying at the end of the night.

outline.heading: Your Lord, your family and your self each have a right
outline.gist: Salman's statement to give every rightful claimant its due, which the Prophet confirmed.

outline.heading: Abu al-Darda's imbalance and Salman's experience
outline.gist: Abu al-Darda had abandoned his wife for constant fasting and prayer; Salman, a lifelong seeker of truth, saw it was unbalanced.

outline.heading: Religiosity requires balance
outline.gist: The most religious person honours the rights of Allah, family, relatives and body together.

outline.heading: The Prophet confirms Salman
outline.gist: Abu al-Darda brings the matter to the Prophet, who affirms that extra worship without balance is not his way.

outline.heading: The full narration in Bukhari
outline.gist: He reads the complete hadith text as recorded by al-Bukhari.

themes.label: Moderation and balance (wasatiyyah)
themes.note: True religiosity balances the rights of Allah, family and self.

themes.label: Marriage and the relationship between spouses
themes.note: Neglecting one's spouse in the name of worship violates her right.

themes.label: Brotherhood, companionship and friendship
themes.note: A true brother visits, notices and corrects with wisdom.

themes.label: The companions and the early generations
themes.note: Salman's background as a seasoned seeker of truth gave him insight into balance.

hadith.gist: The Prophet paired Salman and Abu al-Darda as brothers; Salman found Abu al-Darda neglecting his wife through constant fasting and night prayer, told him his Lord, family and self each have a right, and the Prophet said Salman spoke the truth.

maxims: Give every one with a right their due

stories.point: Worship that neglects family and body is unbalanced; the Prophet endorsed Salman's correction.

takeaways: Give your Lord, your family and your body each their rightful share.
Do not let voluntary worship cause you to neglect your spouse.
Correct a brother gently and practically, as Salman did.
Measure religiosity by balance, not by quantity of extra acts.

49:2.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ لَا تَرۡفَعُوٓاْ أَصۡوَٰتَكُمۡ فَوۡقَ صَوۡتِ ٱلنَّبِيِّ وَلَا تَجۡهَرُواْ لَهُۥ بِٱلۡقَوۡلِ كَجَهۡرِ بَعۡضِكُمۡ لِبَعۡضٍ أَن تَحۡبَطَ أَعۡمَٰلُكُمۡ وَأَنتُمۡ لَا تَشۡعُرُونَ
49:2.en: O ye who believe! Lift not up your voices above the voice of the Prophet, nor shout when speaking to him as ye shout one to another, lest your works be rendered vain while ye perceive not

pYCsGiKyHXs.title: Moderation #2
pYCsGiKyHXs.one_line: The hadith warning against ghuluw in religion: why imbalance inside our religiosity is the most damaging kind and how to find the sweet spot.
pYCsGiKyHXs.summary: The sheikh continues his moderation series with a short hadith he wants people to memorize: the Prophet's warning, beware of ghuluw in the religion. He explains the opening word as a warning to stay away, and traces ghuluw to a root used for prices rising beyond what is affordable and water boiling until it loses control. Ghuluw is misjudging something's worth, giving it more or less than it deserves. Everyone misbalances parts of life, he says, and Islam exists to teach balance, but imbalance inside religiosity itself is the worst place for it. His example is reverence for the Prophet: fall below the proper respect, as the Quran warns about raising voices to him, and deeds lose their value; go beyond it and you repeat what was done with Isa. The right point is not a mathematical middle between two wrong answers but the correct answer itself. He describes people who overemphasize the mechanics of practice or the spirituality and end up walking through Islam with a limp. Finding the balance takes education, dedication and attention, and it is central to the religion.

outline.heading: Moderation as central to Islam
outline.gist: Balance is one of the main values of Islam and the Quran's whole teaching; he introduces a short hadith on it.

outline.heading: Iyyakum: a warning to stay away
outline.gist: The word means beware, and the warning is against ghuluw.

outline.heading: Ghuluw: prices and boiling water
outline.gist: The root describes things going beyond what is acceptable; ghuluw is giving something more or less than it deserves.

outline.heading: Religion is the worst place to lose balance
outline.gist: Humans always misjudge priorities in life, but exaggeration inside the religion is the most harmful.

outline.heading: Reverence for the Prophet as a test of balance
outline.gist: Too little respect voids deeds, as with raising voices to him; too much repeats what was done with Isa.

outline.heading: The sweet spot is not the median
outline.gist: The balanced answer is right in itself, not a midpoint between two wrong answers.

outline.heading: Walking in Islam with a limp
outline.gist: Overemphasizing mechanics or spirituality breaks balance; getting it right needs education and attention.

outline.heading: Outro

12:21.ar: وَقَالَ ٱلَّذِي ٱشۡتَرَىٰهُ مِن مِّصۡرَ لِٱمۡرَأَتِهِۦٓ أَكۡرِمِي مَثۡوَىٰهُ عَسَىٰٓ أَن يَنفَعَنَآ أَوۡ نَتَّخِذَهُۥ وَلَدࣰ اۚ وَكَذَٰلِكَ مَكَّنَّا لِيُوسُفَ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَلِنُعَلِّمَهُۥ مِن تَأۡوِيلِ ٱلۡأَحَادِيثِۚ وَٱللَّهُ غَالِبٌ عَلَىٰٓ أَمۡرِهِۦ وَلَٰكِنَّ أَكۡثَرَ ٱلنَّاسِ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ
12:21.en: And he of Egypt who purchased him said unto his wife: Receive him honourably. Perchance he may prove useful to us or we may adopt him as a son. Thus we established Joseph in the land that We might teach him the interpretation of events. And Allah was predominant in His career, but most of mankind know not

12:22.ar: وَلَمَّا بَلَغَ أَشُدَّهُۥٓ ءَاتَيۡنَٰهُ حُكۡمࣰ ا وَعِلۡمࣰ اۚ وَكَذَٰلِكَ نَجۡزِي ٱلۡمُحۡسِنِينَ
12:22.en: And And when he reached his prime We gave him wisdom and knowledge. Thus We reward the good

12:23.ar: وَرَٰوَدَتۡهُ ٱلَّتِي هُوَ فِي بَيۡتِهَا عَن نَّفۡسِهِۦ وَغَلَّقَتِ ٱلۡأَبۡوَٰبَ وَقَالَتۡ هَيۡتَ لَكَۚ قَالَ مَعَاذَ ٱللَّهِۖ إِنَّهُۥ رَبِّيٓ أَحۡسَنَ مَثۡوَايَۖ إِنَّهُۥ لَا يُفۡلِحُ ٱلظَّٰلِمُونَ
12:23.en: And she, in whose house he was, asked of him an evil act. She bolted the doors and said: Come! He said: I seek refuge in Allah! Lo! he is my lord, who hath treated me honourably. Lo! wrong-doers never prosper

12:24.ar: وَلَقَدۡ هَمَّتۡ بِهِۦۖ وَهَمَّ بِهَا لَوۡلَآ أَن رَّءَا بُرۡهَٰنَ رَبِّهِۦۚ كَذَٰلِكَ لِنَصۡرِفَ عَنۡهُ ٱلسُّوٓءَ وَٱلۡفَحۡشَآءَۚ إِنَّهُۥ مِنۡ عِبَادِنَا ٱلۡمُخۡلَصِينَ
12:24.en: She verily desired him, and he would have desired her if it had not been that he saw the argument of his Lord. Thus it was, that We might ward off from him evil and lewdness. Lo! he was of Our chosen slaves

12:25.ar: وَٱسۡتَبَقَا ٱلۡبَابَ وَقَدَّتۡ قَمِيصَهُۥ مِن دُبُرࣲ وَأَلۡفَيَا سَيِّدَهَا لَدَا ٱلۡبَابِۚ قَالَتۡ مَا جَزَآءُ مَنۡ أَرَادَ بِأَهۡلِكَ سُوٓءًا إِلَّآ أَن يُسۡجَنَ أَوۡ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمࣱ‏
12:25.en: And they raced with one another to the door, and she tore his shirt from behind, and they met her lord and master at the door. She said: What shall be his reward, who wisheth evil to thy folk, save prison or a painful doom

12:26.ar: قَالَ هِيَ رَٰوَدَتۡنِي عَن نَّفۡسِيۚ وَشَهِدَ شَاهِدࣱ مِّنۡ أَهۡلِهَآ إِن كَانَ قَمِيصُهُۥ قُدَّ مِن قُبُلࣲ فَصَدَقَتۡ وَهُوَ مِنَ ٱلۡكَٰذِبِينَ
12:26.en: (Joseph) said: She it was who asked of me an evil act. And a witness of her own folk testified: If his shirt is torn from before, then she speaketh truth and he is of the liars

12:27.ar: وَإِن كَانَ قَمِيصُهُۥ قُدَّ مِن دُبُرࣲ فَكَذَبَتۡ وَهُوَ مِنَ ٱلصَّٰدِقِينَ
12:27.en: And if his shirt is torn from behind, then she hath lied and he is of the truthful

12:28.ar: فَلَمَّا رَءَا قَمِيصَهُۥ قُدَّ مِن دُبُرࣲ قَالَ إِنَّهُۥ مِن كَيۡدِكُنَّۖ إِنَّ كَيۡدَكُنَّ عَظِيمࣱ‏
12:28.en: So when he saw his shirt torn from behind, he said: Lo! this is of the guile of you women. Lo! the guile of you is very great

12:29.ar: يُوسُفُ أَعۡرِضۡ عَنۡ هَٰذَاۚ وَٱسۡتَغۡفِرِي لِذَنۢبِكِۖ إِنَّكِ كُنتِ مِنَ ٱلۡخَاطِـِٔينَ
12:29.en: O Joseph! Turn away from this, and thou, (O woman), ask forgiveness for thy sin. Lo! thou art of the faulty

12:37.ar: قَالَ لَا يَأۡتِيكُمَا طَعَامࣱ تُرۡزَقَانِهِۦٓ إِلَّا نَبَّأۡتُكُمَا بِتَأۡوِيلِهِۦ قَبۡلَ أَن يَأۡتِيَكُمَاۚ ذَٰلِكُمَا مِمَّا عَلَّمَنِي رَبِّيٓۚ إِنِّي تَرَكۡتُ مِلَّةَ قَوۡمࣲ لَّا يُؤۡمِنُونَ بِٱللَّهِ وَهُم بِٱلۡأٓخِرَةِ هُمۡ كَٰفِرُونَ
12:37.en: He said: The food which ye are given (daily) shall not come unto you but I shall tell you the interpretation ere it cometh unto you. This is of that which my Lord hath taught me. Lo! I have forsaken the religion of folk who believe not in Allah and are disbelievers in the Hereafter

12:38.ar: وَٱتَّبَعۡتُ مِلَّةَ ءَابَآءِيٓ إِبۡرَٰهِيمَ وَإِسۡحَٰقَ وَيَعۡقُوبَۚ مَا كَانَ لَنَآ أَن نُّشۡرِكَ بِٱللَّهِ مِن شَيۡءࣲۚ ذَٰلِكَ مِن فَضۡلِ ٱللَّهِ عَلَيۡنَا وَعَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ وَلَٰكِنَّ أَكۡثَرَ ٱلنَّاسِ لَا يَشۡكُرُونَ
12:38.en: And I have followed the religion of my fathers, Abraham and Isaac and Jacob. It never was for us to attribute aught as partner to Allah. This is of the bounty of Allah unto us (the seed of Abraham) and unto mankind; but most men give not thanks

12:39.ar: يَٰصَٰحِبَيِ ٱلسِّجۡنِ ءَأَرۡبَابࣱ مُّتَفَرِّقُونَ خَيۡرٌ أَمِ ٱللَّهُ ٱلۡوَٰحِدُ ٱلۡقَهَّارُ
12:39.en: O my fellow-prisoners! Are divers lords better, or Allah the One, Almighty

105:1.ar: أَلَمۡ تَرَ كَيۡفَ فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ بِأَصۡحَٰبِ ٱلۡفِيلِ
105:1.en: Hast thou not seen how thy Lord dealt with the owners of the Elephant

17:32.ar: وَلَا تَقۡرَبُواْ ٱلزِّنَىٰٓۖ إِنَّهُۥ كَانَ فَٰحِشَةࣰ وَسَآءَ سَبِيلࣰ ا
17:32.en: And come not near unto adultery. Lo! it is an abomination and an evil way

33:14.ar: وَلَوۡ دُخِلَتۡ عَلَيۡهِم مِّنۡ أَقۡطَارِهَا ثُمَّ سُئِلُواْ ٱلۡفِتۡنَةَ لَأٓتَوۡهَا وَمَا تَلَبَّثُواْ بِهَآ إِلَّا يَسِيرࣰ ا
33:14.en: If the enemy had entered from all sides and they had been exhorted to treachery, they would have committed it, and would have hesitated thereupon but little

4:66.ar: وَلَوۡ أَنَّا كَتَبۡنَا عَلَيۡهِمۡ أَنِ ٱقۡتُلُوٓاْ أَنفُسَكُمۡ أَوِ ٱخۡرُجُواْ مِن دِيَٰرِكُم مَّا فَعَلُوهُ إِلَّا قَلِيلࣱ مِّنۡهُمۡۖ وَلَوۡ أَنَّهُمۡ فَعَلُواْ مَا يُوعَظُونَ بِهِۦ لَكَانَ خَيۡرࣰ ا لَّهُمۡ وَأَشَدَّ تَثۡبِيتࣰ ا
4:66.en: And if We had decreed for them: Lay down your lives or go forth from your dwellings, but few of them would have done it; though if they did what they are exhorted to do it would be better for them, and more strengthening

12:17.ar: قَالُواْ يَٰٓأَبَانَآ إِنَّا ذَهَبۡنَا نَسۡتَبِقُ وَتَرَكۡنَا يُوسُفَ عِندَ مَتَٰعِنَا فَأَكَلَهُ ٱلذِّئۡبُۖ وَمَآ أَنتَ بِمُؤۡمِنࣲ لَّنَا وَلَوۡ كُنَّا صَٰدِقِينَ
12:17.en: Saying: O our father! We went racing one with another, and left Joseph by our things, and the wolf devoured him, and thou believest not our saying even when we speak the truth

12:53.ar: ۞وَمَآ أُبَرِّئُ نَفۡسِيٓۚ إِنَّ ٱلنَّفۡسَ لَأَمَّارَةُۢ بِٱلسُّوٓءِ إِلَّا مَا رَحِمَ رَبِّيٓۚ إِنَّ رَبِّي غَفُورࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
12:53.en: I do not exculpate myself. Lo! the (human) soul enjoineth unto evil, save that whereon my Lord hath mercy. Lo! my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful

7Xgg9ido_Ks.title: Arabic Tafseer: Surah Yusuf (12:22-29)
7Xgg9ido_Ks.one_line: Yusuf and the wife of al-Aziz: every cause of temptation gathered, yet he refused because he had already seen his Lord's proof.
7Xgg9ido_Ks.summary: The sheikh resumes the episode of Yusuf and the wife of al-Aziz and lists every factor that made falling into zina easy: Yusuf was a slave with no reputation to lose, a young man, behind locked doors, pursued rather than pursuing, dependent on her power, and she was young and beautiful. Yet the only question for a believer is whether an act pleases Allah. Yusuf's answer gives three barriers: seeking refuge in Allah, loyalty to the man who honoured him, and the universal rule that wrongdoers never succeed. From this he argues that character is fixed and does not rise and fall with circumstances. His central point is verse 24: Yusuf did not incline to her because he had already seen his Lord's proof, a certainty of mind and heart built over his life, not a vision in the moment, and he rejects Isra'iliyyat to the contrary. He separates inclination, intention and wishing, explains that zina has preliminaries, and distinguishes the man who avoids sin from conviction from the one who simply lacks opportunity. He warns against reading tafsir or hadith without a teacher, then explains the race to the door, the torn shirt, the accusation and the witness whose forensic reasoning cleared Yusuf. He asks parents to start with belief so children reach that certainty.

outline.heading: Opening
Recap: Yusuf and the wife of al-Aziz
outline.gist: He returns to the episode of Zulaykha begun last week and the real difficulty in understanding it.

outline.heading: Given judgement and knowledge, yet a slave
outline.gist: Yusuf reached maturity with strong reasoning and knowledge from his father, but on paper he was a slave.

outline.heading: The man called by a woman of status and beauty
outline.gist: The hadith of the seven under Allah's shade alludes to Yusuf's stand.

outline.heading: First cause: no reputation at stake
outline.gist: As a slave nobody would hold him to account, so fear for his name could not restrain him.

outline.heading: Second cause: youth
outline.gist: A young man has less control over desire than a mature adult.

outline.heading: Third cause: the closed doors
outline.gist: She hid him from every eye, removing his natural shyness and fear of exposure.

outline.heading: Fourth cause: she pursued him
outline.gist: She sought him; he did not seek her.

outline.heading: Fifth cause: his life depended on her
outline.gist: She held power in the house and threatened him; she was also young and beautiful, close to his age.

outline.heading: Every cause gathered, while people today chase sin
outline.gist: Today people work around every barrier to reach the haram; Yusuf had it handed to him.

outline.heading: No risk to him, and even leverage
outline.gist: She was the one who feared scandal, so he could even have used it against her.

outline.heading: The only question: does it please Allah?
outline.gist: The believer is spared endless calculations of risk and cost; if it angers Allah the matter is closed.

outline.heading: Rawadathu, ghallaqat, hayta lak
outline.gist: The verse describes the scene clearly in chaste language; she had prepared herself for him.

outline.heading: A proof against men until the Last Day
outline.gist: Because it happened, no man can claim he had no way out of zina.

outline.heading: Ma'adh Allah: an immediate refusal
outline.gist: He rejects readings that suggest Yusuf weakened; his answer was instant.

outline.heading: First barrier: refuge in Allah
outline.gist: He seeks refuge in Allah from what angers Him.

outline.heading: Second barrier: loyalty to the one who honoured him
outline.gist: Al-Aziz honoured him; Yusuf keeps the loyalty his own brothers denied their father.

outline.heading: Character does not fluctuate
outline.gist: Character has no ebb and flow; once adopted it is kept until one meets Allah, and he admits he does not yet know how to teach this to youth.

outline.heading: Generous only when rich is an opportunist
outline.gist: The amount may change with circumstances, but the trait itself stays constant.

outline.heading: The only story told unbroken
outline.gist: Surah Yusuf tells one story start to finish, unlike the stories of Musa or Ibrahim.

outline.heading: Steadfastness is the lesson
outline.gist: The story is not only about a man invited to sin but about staying the same under every pressure.

outline.heading: Third barrier: wrongdoers never succeed
outline.gist: A general understanding of existence: tyrants end in the rubbish heap of history.

outline.heading: Source of his strength: his father's teaching
outline.gist: His values came from Yaqub's upbringing and the knowledge Allah gave him.

outline.heading: Wa laqad hammat bihi: where to pause
outline.gist: One should stop after her intention, since joining the phrases misleads the listener.

outline.heading: The proof was seen earlier, not in the moment
outline.gist: Reading it as a sudden vision contradicts the previous verse; the Quran explains itself.

outline.heading: Law la: prevention through a prior cause
outline.gist: Because he had seen the proof, inclining to her never happened.

outline.heading: Inclination, intention and wishful thinking
outline.gist: Hamm precedes intention; intention is firm resolve; a wish carries no reward or sin.

outline.heading: A burhan is not seen with the eyes
outline.gist: Burhan means a rational proof, seen by mind and heart.

outline.heading: Rejecting the Isra'iliyyat
outline.gist: Stories of him seeing his father's face contradict the Quran and are rejected.

outline.heading: Zina has preliminaries: fortify yourself beforehand
outline.gist: Nobody falls suddenly; it comes step by step through eyes, ears and wishes, hence the command not to approach zina.

outline.heading: Evidence from his words in prison
outline.gist: Months later he declares he follows the creed of his fathers, showing his long-held certainty.

outline.heading: Seeing as the Prophet saw the Elephant army
outline.gist: The Prophet saw what happened to Abraha's army through reports and its blind survivors, not with his own eyes.

outline.heading: She certainly intended; he would have, but for the proof
outline.gist: The lam and qad confirm her intent; he was protected beforehand.

outline.heading: Linasrifa 'anhu: equipped to turn evil away
outline.gist: Allah did not keep temptation from him; He prepared him to turn it away himself.

outline.heading: Among Our devoted servants
outline.gist: Al-mukhlasin are those Allah purified for Himself by filling their hearts with sincerity.

outline.heading: Two kinds of people who avoid sin
outline.gist: One saw the proof of his Lord; the other simply lacks opportunity; the same holds for haram money.

outline.heading: The most important phrase in the surah
outline.gist: Character only comes from seeing the proof; many of us are fine only because Allah has covered us.

outline.heading: How do we instil this in our children?
outline.gist: He asks openly how to bring this fortification to hearts and minds.

outline.heading: Three barriers against a thousand excuses
outline.gist: Religion, loyalty and wisdom each stood as a dam between Yusuf and sin.

outline.heading: Interpretations that cast doubt on Yusuf
outline.gist: Muddying a deep verse turns people away from its meaning, which is Iblis's work.

outline.heading: Encyclopedic tafsirs and weak reports
outline.gist: Al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi collect every report with chains so scholars can know the weak ones.

outline.heading: Read hadith and tafsir with a teacher
outline.gist: Without the tools of Arabic and Quranic sciences, reading alone leads to confusion, as social media shows.

outline.heading: Seeing the proof means certainty in promise and threat
outline.gist: Certainty extends to Allah's promise of paradise and threat of fire, which protects the believer.

outline.heading: Begin with belief
outline.gist: To protect ourselves and our children, start with creed and knowing Allah's majesty.

outline.heading: Question: the one who avoids sin for lack of chance
outline.gist: He declines to rule on the second kind, as scholars have long kept silent out of fear.

outline.heading: The frightening 'if' that Allah knows
outline.gist: Allah knows what people would do if tested; ask for safety and seek the proof of your Lord.

outline.heading: The race to the door and the torn shirt
outline.gist: Recitation of the verse with a note on reading qamis correctly.

outline.heading: Istabaqa: the same word as the brothers' race
outline.gist: His brothers raced to destroy him; now he races away from sin.

outline.heading: Qadd and the meaning of qamis
outline.gist: Qadd is tearing and keeping the torn piece; qamis is any garment worn over the shoulders.

outline.heading: Alfaya sayyidaha: surprised at the last door
outline.gist: Sayyid shows her husband was older and that she was young.

outline.heading: Her accusation and the trials ahead
outline.gist: She immediately accuses him; the story will still test Yusuf's word.

outline.heading: Hiya rawadatni: Yusuf defends himself
outline.gist: Recitation of the next verses.

outline.heading: Two claims before al-Aziz
outline.gist: She claims assault and he says she seduced him; al-Aziz was not alone at the door.

outline.heading: Who the witness was
outline.gist: A relative of hers, likely the head of police, while al-Aziz oversaw the treasury.

outline.heading: Forensic reasoning from the shirt
outline.gist: A tear in front means he advanced; a tear behind means he fled.

outline.heading: Why her claim was tested first
outline.gist: In such cases the claim of the woman is examined first; an unmarried man alone with a woman is already blameworthy.

outline.heading: Surah Yusuf's many sciences
outline.gist: The surah contains criminal investigation and economic planning, and Yusuf learned from this man too.

outline.heading: Inna kaydakunna 'azim
outline.gist: The witness concludes it was her scheme, tells Yusuf to drop it and her to seek forgiveness.

outline.heading: Outro

quran.point: Yusuf's words in prison show his long-held tawhid, the proof he had already seen.
Many lords or Allah the One: his settled conviction.
Seeing can mean knowing with certainty without eyesight.
Do not approach zina: stay away from its steps.
Allah knows what people would do if put to the test.
Had it been prescribed, few would have obeyed: the frightening 'if'.
The brothers used the same word for racing.
The soul inclines to evil, but the believer does not listen to it.

hadith.gist: Among the seven shaded by Allah is a man called by a woman of status and beauty who says, I fear Allah.
Whoever intends a good deed and does it, or intends it and does not do it, is rewarded.
The wise one holds himself to account and works for after death; the weak follows his desires and wishes upon Allah.
Yusuf was given an exceptional share of beauty.

maxims: Character has no ebb and flow
A wish carries neither reward nor sin
The wrongdoer never succeeds
Fortify yourself before the moment, not during it

stories.who: Yusuf and the wife of al-Aziz
stories.point: Every cause of temptation can gather and a believer can still refuse.
Their lack of loyalty contrasts with Yusuf's loyalty to al-Aziz.

stories.who: Abraha's army and its survivors in Mecca
stories.point: Certainty can come without seeing with one's own eyes.
Sound forensic reasoning cleared Yusuf from the torn shirt.

contemporary: Social media as a source of confused religious interpretation
takeaways: Ask only one question before any act: does it please Allah?
Build certainty in Allah, His promise and His threat before temptation comes
Stay away from the preliminaries of zina: looks, talk and wishes
Read hadith and tafsir with a qualified teacher, not alone
Start children's education with belief and knowing Allah

23:115.ar: أَفَحَسِبۡتُمۡ أَنَّمَا خَلَقۡنَٰكُمۡ عَبَثࣰ ا وَأَنَّكُمۡ إِلَيۡنَا لَا تُرۡجَعُونَ
23:115.en: Deemed ye then that We had created you for naught, and that ye would not be returned unto Us

51:56.ar: وَمَا خَلَقۡتُ ٱلۡجِنَّ وَٱلۡإِنسَ إِلَّا لِيَعۡبُدُونِ
51:56.en: I created the jinn and humankind only that they might worship Me

11:118.ar: وَلَوۡ شَآءَ رَبُّكَ لَجَعَلَ ٱلنَّاسَ أُمَّةࣰ وَٰحِدَةࣰۖ وَلَا يَزَالُونَ مُخۡتَلِفِينَ
11:118.en: And if thy Lord had willed, He verily would have made mankind one nation, yet they cease not differing

11:119.ar: إِلَّا مَن رَّحِمَ رَبُّكَۚ وَلِذَٰلِكَ خَلَقَهُمۡۗ وَتَمَّتۡ كَلِمَةُ رَبِّكَ لَأَمۡلَأَنَّ جَهَنَّمَ مِنَ ٱلۡجِنَّةِ وَٱلنَّاسِ أَجۡمَعِينَ
11:119.en: Save him on whom thy Lord hath mercy; and for that He did create them. And the Word of thy Lord hath been fulfilled: Verily I shall fill hell with the jinn and mankind together

49:13.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ إِنَّا خَلَقۡنَٰكُم مِّن ذَكَرࣲ وَأُنثَىٰ وَجَعَلۡنَٰكُمۡ شُعُوبࣰ ا وَقَبَآئِلَ لِتَعَارَفُوٓاْۚ إِنَّ أَكۡرَمَكُمۡ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ أَتۡقَىٰكُمۡۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ خَبِيرࣱ‏
49:13.en: O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another. Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct. Lo! Allah is Knower, Aware

10:32.ar: فَذَٰلِكُمُ ٱللَّهُ رَبُّكُمُ ٱلۡحَقُّۖ فَمَاذَا بَعۡدَ ٱلۡحَقِّ إِلَّا ٱلضَّلَٰلُۖ فَأَنَّىٰ تُصۡرَفُونَ
10:32.en: Such then is Allah, your rightful Lord. After the Truth what is there saving error? How then are ye turned away

WBiHeop_nU0.speaker: adnan
WBiHeop_nU0.speaker_note: Continues his own series ('I talked about the first point, moral integrity') and speaks as the regular MWN khatib.
WBiHeop_nU0.title: The Implications of Knowing: Finding Meaning
WBiHeop_nU0.one_line: In his series on knowing Allah, the second implication is meaning: a believer who knows his purpose cannot be bored or empty.
WBiHeop_nU0.summary: In his series on what knowing Allah must do for a person, he turns from moral integrity to the second implication, meaning. He builds it from the Quran: Allah asks whether we imagined we were created in vain, states that jinn and humans were created only to know and serve Him, explains that human difference and the spread of nations exist so we may know one another and live fully, and calls Himself the Truth beyond which there is only loss. The oldest human fear, a purposeless existence in an expanding void, is not a question a believer has to ask. Meaning produces purpose, purpose produces drive, drive produces behavior; without that chain life is a void that money, travel, drugs or pleasure only make hungrier. Even unbelievers who invent a meaning find fulfillment, so a Muslim who knows God yet is bored or empty is inexplicable. Purpose is found where Allah placed you: Adam was made khalifa, a steward and caregiver, and serving a God who needs nothing means carrying responsibility in your roles as parent, worker, student or professional. The ummah has endless unmet needs. In the second khutbah he warns against turning the things created for our use, food, drink and enjoyment, into the purpose itself, and grieves the chronic emptiness he sees in Muslim youth.

outline.heading: Opening
What must knowing Allah do for you?
outline.gist: Every Muslim should contemplate this until no question remains. The first implication was moral integrity, by far the most important; more points follow.

outline.heading: Point two: meaning. Were you created in vain?
outline.gist: The verse asking whether we imagined we were created without purpose and would not return to Him: Allah is exalted above creating anything meaninglessly.

outline.heading: The Quran repeats it from many angles
outline.gist: Jinn and humans were created to know and serve Him; He chose not to make us all the same but gave us freedom and difference; He made nations and tribes so we may know one another and live life fully.

outline.heading: The oldest human fear, answered
outline.gist: The thinking human has always feared floating in an expanding abyss with no story or legacy; for one who knows Allah this is no longer a question or a doubt.

outline.heading: Allah is al-Haqq, the granter of meaning
outline.gist: Al-Haqq is meaningfulness as opposed to falsehood; beyond the Truth there is only purposelessness and loss, so believers do not carry that struggle.

outline.heading: Meaning, purpose, drive, action, and the void
outline.gist: Without that chain life is empty however much fun or wealth it holds; money, travel, friends, drugs and sex only make the void hungrier.

outline.heading: How can a Muslim who knows God be bored?
outline.gist: Even people without God find fulfillment once they give life a cause, so a believer who is bored is inexplicable, unless he has already achieved everything Allah put him on earth for.

outline.heading: Boredom and meaning do not come together
outline.gist: The early Arabic sources and the Prophet barely use a word for boredom; the hadith on free time is about having time, not emptiness.

outline.heading: Find purpose where Allah placed you
outline.gist: Not everyone needs a jubba and a minbar; the specifics of your life were crafted for you so you can serve Allah through them.

outline.heading: The first topical verse: Adam made for the earth
outline.gist: After al-Fatihah and the introduction of al-Baqarah, verse 30 states human purpose at once: Adam was destined for the earth before he did anything, wherever his first Jannah was.

outline.heading: Khalifa means steward and caregiver
outline.gist: Not a political term in the Quran but one responsible for something on behalf of another: the earth, yourself and those around you.

outline.heading: Serving One who needs nothing: your roles
outline.gist: Allah needs nothing we have, so service takes the form of responsibility as parent, sibling, employee, doctor or cab driver; go to work as the service you bring rather than hoping for a pot of gold.

outline.heading: Destined for Jannah: the question is how
outline.gist: Purpose can be low or harmful, but knowing God rules that out; you are destined for greatness and only search for the way to fulfill it, which is underrated among the youth.

outline.heading: The ummah's unmet needs
outline.gist: Meaning is easy to find because the ummah falls short on every front: the local community and its youth, advocacy for Muslims here and abroad, the oppressed in Palestine and Sudan.

outline.heading: Philanthropists without God live more meaningfully
outline.gist: He has met people who invented a meaning they think leads nowhere and still find fulfillment, while Muslims who know Allah need getaways to feel joy.

outline.heading: Interlude
Don't make what was created for you your purpose
outline.gist: The Quran says mountains, rivers, sun, moon and stars were created for you; living to eat and enjoy turns the means into the end and steps down from the status Allah gave you.

outline.heading: Meaning is no ghost hunt
outline.gist: Once you know He is al-Haqq, meaning is among the first things you find. Would Palestine or any part of the Muslim world be in this state if two billion Muslims lived with purpose?

outline.heading: The chronic emptiness of our youth
outline.gist: A numbness he sees especially in young people with potential who just eat, sleep and repeat; Muslims should never live that way.

outline.heading: Outro

6OG8bxEFN4Y.title: Tazkiyah Halaqah: Self-Value, Episode 42
6OG8bxEFN4Y.one_line: From vanity to arrogance (kibr): ranking ourselves against others, racism as collective arrogance, humility as plain reality, and Iblis's refusal.
6OG8bxEFN4Y.summary: He closes vanity with clarifications. Vanity and arrogance swing together; vanity is claiming to know how much credit our effort earned, while the confident person says alhamdulillah. Fake humility performed for admiration only feeds vanity. Knowing you are good at something is not vanity if it is objective, properly certified, and does not move your worth; as a physician he knows his field, but cures come from Allah. People who anchor worth to nation, race or family name are shaken when those fail, as Palestinians and Iraqis learned; a Muslim anchors worth to Allah, the only true constant. Arrogance differs from vanity in needing others: it is the ranking we run whenever someone new enters our space, threatening the nafs' survival instinct, so we label them arrogant or hunt for a flaw. Without that need, a more accomplished person becomes a resource rather than a threat. The Prophet warned that an atom's weight of arrogance bars Paradise. Racism is arrogance against whole peoples, as his own childhood prejudice against the neighbouring village showed. Humility is simply acknowledging that we are weak, dependent and equal. He begins Iblis's story: pious enough to dwell among angels, he refused to bow to an untested Adam, and anyone certain they would have obeyed repeats his mistake.

outline.heading: Self-value is inseparable from ethics
outline.gist: The largest module touches everyone, and how we view ourselves shapes the ethics we adopt; tazkiyah and morality cannot be separated.

outline.heading: Four diseases under one umbrella; vanity recapped
outline.gist: Vanity, arrogance, showing off and envy mirror each other; vanity swings worth upward by claiming credit, out of fear of low self-esteem.

outline.heading: Vanity and arrogance always come together
outline.gist: He has never seen a credible case of one without the other, hence the two-storey pendulum; the opposite of vanity is confidence in Allah-given potential.

outline.heading: No one knows their share of an outcome
outline.gist: Even scientifically one can only guess the percentage owed to effort; assigning it is taking on Allah's role of judgement.

outline.heading: Intention cannot be measured; 'I did it' versus 'alhamdulillah'
outline.gist: Sincerity and integrity behind effort decide reward and are beyond science, so credit success to Allah and ask Him to accept.

outline.heading: Fake humility feeds vanity
outline.gist: Performing humility to be admired is among the ugliest traits and shows how the nafs manipulates even ourselves.

outline.heading: Who is worthy of praise?
outline.gist: The Quran's first word answers it: praise belongs to Allah by nature, while we are praiseworthy only if He declares it.

outline.heading: Knowing you are good at something is not vanity
outline.gist: Recognizing a skill is needed; the problem begins only when that knowledge raises or lowers your sense of worth.

outline.heading: The physician knows his field, but Allah cures
outline.gist: He can say he knows a disease and how to treat it, while patients' recovery is not his to claim.

outline.heading: Competence must be certified
outline.gist: Islamic learning rests on ijazah just as medicine rests on licensing; self-appointed preachers have no one vouching for them.

outline.heading: Secure worth lets you take feedback
outline.gist: People with stable worth improve openly; many non-Muslims achieve this by anchoring worth to something they consider constant.

outline.heading: Anchoring worth to nation, race or family name
outline.gist: These seem constant but can collapse, as when a family name is disgraced.

outline.heading: When the anchor breaks: Palestine and Iraq
outline.gist: Those expelled in 1948 and Iraqis after the invasion saw identity shattered; a Muslim anchored to Allah cannot be shaken, good servant or bad.

outline.heading: Good assumptions about others in a healthy society
outline.gist: Praise and thank others for their efforts while asking Allah to credit your own; most of the world does the reverse.

outline.heading: Kibr requires someone else
outline.gist: Vanity is between you and yourself; arrogance involves comparison with others, which is most of social life.

outline.heading: The person raised alone on an island
outline.gist: Only someone who never met another human could be vain without being arrogant, a question scholars and psychologists have pondered.

outline.heading: Humility is the second storey; self-hatred is its mirror
outline.gist: Arrogance concerns how we see others; in Canada he found many people beating themselves up over failures, which is the opposite swing.

outline.heading: Review success and failure objectively
outline.gist: Neither pat yourself on the back nor hate yourself: note what to repeat, what to avoid, and praise Allah.

outline.heading: Arrogance is the private ranking system
outline.gist: With variable worth we rank everyone we meet to place ourselves above them; when we fail to, envy is born.

outline.heading: Newcomers threaten the nafs
outline.gist: Like mammals, we feel threatened by a new person because the nafs sees a competitor for food, status and survival.

outline.heading: Instant dislike and the label 'arrogant'
outline.gist: We fill gaps in a stranger's story with assumptions and reduce them to one word to justify our feelings.

outline.heading: Hunting for a flaw
outline.gist: At the gym a stronger newcomer draws cold shoulders and scrutiny; each added virtue bothers us more until one flaw is found and inflated.

outline.heading: From threat to resource
outline.gist: Needing to be better than people guarantees feeling worse; without that need, the more accomplished person becomes a mentor.

outline.heading: Seek out people more advanced than you
outline.gist: Objectively we benefit from being surrounded by better people, unless we draw worth from being ahead.

outline.heading: An atom's weight of arrogance
outline.gist: Among the few things said to bar Paradise, arrogance signals a systemic misunderstanding of oneself and others that cannot enter Paradise.

outline.heading: Racism at the heart of conflicts
outline.gist: Palestine, Syria, Africa and North America's conflicts, and empires' invasions, rest on one group seeing another as innately evil.

outline.heading: His village and the village next door
outline.gist: He was raised to see an indistinguishable neighbouring village as savages, until shared high school showed they were better educated than his own.

outline.heading: Everyone has a group they write off
outline.gist: Every listener holds some group to be uniquely bad; generalizations about whole populations are almost always wrong, and racism is arrogance toward a whole people.

outline.heading: The Prophet's humility, and 'I am humble'
outline.gist: He truly saw himself as no better than any creation; a scholarly saying warns that claiming humility implies having stepped down from above.

outline.heading: Humility is acknowledging reality
outline.gist: We come from soil, are weak and dependent, and equal except in taqwa; Allah is al-Mutakabbir by nature, so humility fits us and not Him.

outline.heading: Question: humility is not lowering yourself
outline.gist: Islam defines humility as recognizing the truth that we are all the same, requiring no effort or pose.

outline.heading: Waiting to be proven special
outline.gist: Many secretly feel they are special and await recognition; any good idea or opportunity is Allah's gift, not innate superiority.

outline.heading: Iblis and Pharaoh: stories of origin
outline.gist: The two clearest Quranic cases of arrogance recur in some forty places; Adam's story teaches the enduring pattern of our struggles.

outline.heading: Iblis's freedom and extraordinary piety
outline.gist: A jinn able to disobey, he chose obedience so fully that he was raised among the angels, a rank no human has reached.

outline.heading: The angels' question about a new creation
outline.gist: Knowing the jinn's corruption and bloodshed, the angels asked why create another being free to disobey.

outline.heading: Adam honoured for potential alone
outline.gist: Adam showed only his capacity to learn the names, and the angels were told to bow before he had done any worship.

outline.heading: Iblis could not bring himself to bow
outline.gist: Directly commanded, and knowing Allah well, he did not challenge Allah but found himself unable to obey.

outline.heading: Iblis's argument: merit and nature
outline.gist: Adam had no merit while he had much, and by nature fire seemed above foul clay, so he saw no reason to honour him.

outline.heading: Would you have bowed?
outline.gist: Answering 'certainly' repeats Iblis's arrogance; the lesson is to ask whether you could fail the same way and change that in yourself.

CsuSgyWXi3Y.title: Moderation #1
CsuSgyWXi3Y.one_line: Through the companion who vowed to stand in the sun, stay silent and fast, the Prophet shows no one may invent new worship.
CsuSgyWXi3Y.summary: The sheikh opens a short series on moderation (wasatiyyah), a value he has been working on with the mentorship groups. He uses the hadith of a companion the Prophet noticed standing in the sun while others sat. The man had vowed to stand and never sit, to avoid shade, to stop speaking and to fast. The sheikh stresses that this was a good man who simply wanted to get closer to Allah by giving up comforts. The Prophet told him to sit, take the shade and speak, and to complete his fast. The point is that the man had added new items to the roster of worship. Silence as devotion existed in earlier scripture, as with Maryam, but not in this religion. Fasting is a real act of worship, so that part stayed. The sheikh draws the rule that no one has the right to add acts of worship to Islam: the Prophet already taught exactly how to please Allah, and invented devotions cause harm, open the door to extremism and empty the religion of its essence. He notes that this was one of the rare areas where the Prophet became sharply assertive, and asks listeners to stay within the forms of worship they were given.
